spec.premise: the speaker addresses a house being sold

set.title: To the House on Tenney Street, Before the Closing
set.headnote: In this poem, the speaker addresses the house where she grew up on the day before it is sold.

blueprint.speaker: A grown daughter, now middle-aged, who has come back to empty her dead or departed parents' house in a small Midwestern town the day before the sale closes
blueprint.addressee: The house itself (apostrophe), addressed as 'you' throughout
blueprint.situation: In 1957 the speaker tapes boxes and rolls rugs in the house her father built in 1931. As she goes, she remembers what the thick walls kept in: her father's violence toward her mother, which she covered as a child by turning up the radio. Tomorrow a young couple will move in and praise how quiet the house is.
blueprint.central_idea: The house's famous soundness, the thick walls that kept trouble in, matches the speaker's own lifelong habit of not hearing and not looking. Her calm departure without looking back is the same skill she learned at the radio dial.
blueprint.complexity: The speaker starts by half-accusing the house, a silent and complicit witness. Then she turns and admits that she was the one who turned the radio up. Her last boast, that she will not look back like Lot's wife, sounds like composure, but the poem has shown that this 'better' upbringing was training in concealment. So her refusal to look back is both a survival skill and a continuation of the harm.
blueprint.form_notes: Twenty-six lines of loose blank verse in five quatrains and a closing six-line stanza, with one clean closing rhyme (mat/that). The third stanza runs on into the fourth so that the reader moves straight from the walls into what they hid. The plain, wry diction of a mid-century domestic poem darkens into confession.
blueprint.setting: A plaster-and-joist house on Tenney Street in a small town, built 1931, emptied in 1957 before its sale; cellar furnace, creaking stair, front room, porch mat
characters: the young buying couple with a baby
blueprint.conflict: Internal: the speaker's wish to blame the house and leave cleanly against her recognition of her own part in the family's silence

devices.quote: the cellar where the furnace, like a bishop,
devices.function: Gives the old furnace a stubborn, robed authority that has outlasted the family

devices.quote: You held all that as a jar holds water.
devices.function: Presents the house as a vessel that contained the trouble completely and passively, without judging it or letting it out

devices.quote: the stair that answers every foot
devices.function: Makes the house audible and responsive, a listener and speaker, which sets up its role as the one who 'heard'

devices.quote: Lot's wife looked back.
devices.function: The biblical woman punished for looking back lets the speaker present her refusal to look back as virtue, which the poem turns into irony

devices.quote: I was raised better than that.
devices.function: Her 'better' upbringing was training in not facing harm; the boast exposes the habit

devices.quote: Good plaster, good joists, a good tight roof
devices.function: The insistent g-sounds imitate the town's confident praise

devices.quote: You were a good house. Everyone said so.
devices.function: Begins the run of 'good' that turns ironic when soundness proves to be concealment

devices.quote: and walls so thick no neighbor ever heard
devices.function: Runs across the stanza break so that the reader falls from the walls into the hidden scene

devices.quote: The agent calls you charming. She means old.
devices.function: The full stop sets up the dry, deflating translation of sales language that marks the speaker's wry opening tone

devices.quote: But I was the one who turned the radio up.
devices.function: Turns the poem from accusing the house to confessing the speaker's own part

devices.quote: the pale squares of floor
devices.function: Untouched floor under the rugs shows what stays preserved beneath surfaces

devices.quote: kept the weather out and kept us in
devices.function: Protection and confinement are the same act

devices.quote: the radio turned up to cover it
devices.function: The radio stands for noise used to drown out harm, and for the speaker's complicity

devices.quote: stand in your front room and praise the quiet
devices.function: The buyers' innocent praise of quiet stands against the quiet that once hid violence

shifts.quote: The agent calls you charming. She means old.
shifts.from: wry, dry humor about real estate language
shifts.to: the beginnings of memory as she uncovers the floor

shifts.quote: what you heard: the chair against the door,
shifts.from: ironic praise of the house's soundness
shifts.to: grave, spare recollection of violence

provenance.note: Original poem written for practice; author and setting are invented.

stanzas: The agent calls you charming. She means old.
She means the stair that answers every foot,
the cellar where the furnace, like a bishop,
sits in its rusted robes and will not die.
I have taped the boxes, I have rolled the rugs
and found beneath them the pale squares of floor
the sun has never touched, as clean as the day
my father nailed the boards down in thirty-one.
You were a good house. Everyone said so.
Good plaster, good joists, a good tight roof
that kept the weather out and kept us in,
and walls so thick no neighbor ever heard
what you heard: the chair against the door,
my mother's voice going small, then smaller,
the radio turned up to cover it.
You held all that as a jar holds water.
But I was the one who turned the radio up.
I was eleven, and I knew the dial.
I knew which station had the loudest band.
So don't think I've come here to accuse you.
Tomorrow a couple up from Marlowe, with a baby,
will stand in your front room and praise the quiet.
They'll mean it as a compliment. I lock you,
slide the key beneath the mat, and walk
down to the car without once turning round.
Lot's wife looked back. I was raised better than that.

items.stem: Placing the speaker's discovery of "the pale squares of floor" ([[r1]]) before the third and fourth stanzas primarily serves to

options.text: anticipate the poem's turn to what the house has hidden under its respectable surfaces
options.label: correct
options.why: The untouched floor under the rugs is the first image of something preserved out of sight. It prepares for the walls that kept the family's trouble from being heard.

options.text: establish the father as a careful craftsman whose labor the speaker wishes the buyers would value
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The father is mentioned only as the one who nailed the boards. The speaker never asks the buyers to value his work, and the poem later suggests his violence.

options.text: suggest that the speaker's childhood in the house was untouched by trouble, as clean as the floor
options.label: reversal
options.why: The word 'clean' tempts this reading, but the next stanzas show a childhood marked by violence and concealment.

options.text: mark the moment at which the speaker decides that she can forgive both parents for the past
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the second stanza mentions forgiveness. The stanza describes packing and uncovering, not a decision about her parents.

refs.quote: found beneath them the pale squares of floor

evidence_quotes: found beneath them the pale squares of floor
and walls so thick no neighbor ever heard

items.stem: The allusion to Lot's wife in the final line ([[r1]]) primarily suggests that the speaker

options.text: dresses up as good upbringing the habit of not facing the past that the poem exposes
options.label: correct
options.why: Lot's wife was punished for looking back. The speaker presents her own refusal to turn around as being 'raised better', but the poem has shown that this upbringing taught her to cover and avoid harm.

options.text: regrets leaving the house and expects to be punished for lingering too long beside it
options.label: reversal
options.why: She walks to the car 'without once turning round'. She does not linger, and she does not express any fear of punishment.

options.text: believes that her family's history is a sin for which the whole town deserves destruction
options.label: too_broad
options.why: This stretches the biblical story into a judgment on the town. Nowhere does the poem condemn the town or call for its destruction.

options.text: is proud of a religious upbringing that has given her the strength to start a new life
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: This takes the boast at face value and misses its irony. The poem gives no sign of religious pride or of a hopeful new life.

evidence_quotes: Lot's wife looked back. I was raised better than that.

items.stem: In the first stanza, the details of the stair ([[r1]]) and the furnace chiefly establish the house as

options.text: aged and audible, with fixtures that respond to and outlast the people living there
options.label: correct
options.why: The agent's 'charming' is translated as 'old'. The stair 'answers every foot', and the furnace 'will not die', so the house is noisy, responsive, and longer-lived than its occupants.

options.text: fashionable and well kept, which is why the agent can honestly call it so charming
options.label: reversal
options.why: The speaker undercuts the agent at once: 'She means old.' The details point to age, not fashion.

options.text: dangerous and neglected, with a furnace that the speaker fears will soon break down
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: 'Will not die' means the furnace keeps going stubbornly. It does not mean the furnace is about to fail.

options.text: sacred to the speaker, a place of worship she links to her religious family's past
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: This reads the bishop simile literally. The comparison describes the furnace's robed, stubborn bulk, not religious worship.

refs.quote: the stair that answers every foot

evidence_quotes: She means the stair that answers every foot,

items.stem: The repetition of "good" in the third stanza ([[r1]]) most directly conveys the speaker's

options.text: echo of the town's praise, which turns ironic once soundness is shown to hide abuse
options.label: correct
options.why: 'Everyone said so' marks the praise as public opinion. The same thick walls that earn the praise are the reason 'no neighbor ever heard', so the word 'good' turns ironic.

options.text: sincere pride in her father's carpentry, which she hopes will help raise the house's price
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The praise leads directly into the hidden violence. The speaker is not proudly selling, and price is never mentioned.

options.text: childlike delight in the house, recovered as she remembers how safe she once felt there
options.label: reversal
options.why: The stanza moves straight from 'good' to what the walls concealed, so the memory is of danger, not safety.

options.text: bitter contempt for neighbors who knew of the family's trouble and chose to ignore it
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The poem says that no neighbor ever heard, so the neighbors did not know. Nothing shows contempt for them.

items.stem: Details throughout the poem indicate that the speaker is

options.text: a grown daughter emptying her parents' house for sale and recalling what she heard there
options.label: correct
options.why: She tapes boxes and rolls rugs, refers to 'my father' and 'my mother', recalls being eleven, and leaves the key before the buyers arrive.

options.text: a real estate agent showing the old house to buyers and privately reflecting on its past
options.label: misread_speaker
options.why: The agent is mentioned in the third person ('She means old'). The speaker refers to her own father and mother.

options.text: a neighbor who lived beside the family and now regrets having ignored the noise next door
options.label: misread_speaker
options.why: The poem says no neighbor ever heard. The speaker was inside the house turning the radio up.

options.text: an eleven-year-old girl helping pack up the house as her family prepares to move away
options.label: partially_right
options.why: She was eleven when the events she remembers took place ('I was eleven'). Now she is an adult, closing up the house alone and driving away.

evidence_quotes: I have taped the boxes, I have rolled the rugs

items.stem: Which of the following statements is the most defensible thesis about the poem as a whole?

options.text: By turning from accusing the house to confessing her own part, the speaker shows that her refusal to look back continues the concealment she grew up in.
options.label: correct
options.why: This covers the volta ('But I was the one') and the ironic closing allusion. It makes a specific, arguable claim that the whole poem supports.

options.text: The poem argues that every house absorbs the feelings of the people who live in it, so that selling a home becomes a way to erase painful memories forever.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: This generalizes to every house and claims an erasure the poem does not support. The memories are vivid and unresolved at the end.

options.text: Through its imagery of boxes, rugs, and keys, the poem depicts the ordinary tedium of moving out and the speaker's relief at finishing a long and tiring job.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: It covers only the surface activity of moving and leaves out the violence, the confession, and the irony of the ending.

options.text: The speaker blames the house for the violence she witnessed as a child, and the poem condemns the neighbors who praised the house while ignoring the family.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The speaker turns from blaming the house to blaming herself ('don't think I've come here to accuse you'), and the neighbors never heard.

evidence_quotes: But I was the one who turned the radio up.
Lot's wife looked back. I was raised better than that.

items.stem: The speaker's first-person account of the events in the fourth stanza ([[r1]]) affects the reader's understanding chiefly by

options.text: limiting the violence to what a child could hear, so its full extent stays implied
options.label: correct
options.why: Everything is given as sound or as a sign of it: a chair against the door, a voice going small, a radio. The reader, like the child, never sees what happened.

options.text: giving a complete and objective record of the father's actions from an outside witness
options.label: reversal
options.why: The account is partial and filtered through a child's ears. The father's actions are never described directly.

options.text: revealing the mother's private thoughts about her marriage directly through her own words
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The mother never speaks in the poem. Only her voice 'going small' is reported.

options.text: shifting the focus to the house's own point of view, since the house is the one that heard
options.label: misread_speaker
options.why: The speaker addresses the house as 'you', but the account stays hers. The house never narrates.

my mother's voice going small, then smaller,

items.stem: The simile "You held all that as a jar holds water" ([[r1]]) presents the house as

options.text: a vessel that contained the family's trouble wholly, neither judging nor spilling it
options.label: correct
options.why: A jar holds whatever is poured into it, completely and without choice. The house kept everything inside its walls, which is why no neighbor heard.

options.text: a source of renewal that nourished and sustained the family through its hardest years
options.label: reversal
options.why: Water can suggest nourishment, but here what the house held is violence. The comparison is about containment, not renewal.

options.text: a fragile object that was always close to cracking under the strain of what it held
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The poem stresses the house's solidity ('walls so thick'). Nothing suggests it was about to break.

options.text: a deliberate protector that chose to hide the family's secret in order to spare the child
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The house did contain the secret, but a jar does not choose anything. The simile stresses passive holding, not intention.

refs.quote: You held all that as a jar holds water.

evidence_quotes: You held all that as a jar holds water.
and walls so thick no neighbor ever heard

items.stem: In context, the phrase "going small, then smaller" ([[r1]]) primarily conveys

options.text: the mother's gradual diminishment, as registered by a listener who could not see it
options.label: correct
options.why: The child knows the mother only through her voice. Its shrinking signals her being overpowered, without the poem describing the violence directly.

options.text: the mother's growing distance as she walked away from the speaker into another room
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: This treats 'small' as physical distance. In the stanza's context of a barred door and covering noise, it signals the mother being diminished.

options.text: the speaker's impatience with a mother whose complaints she had learned to ignore
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Nothing in the line is impatient or dismissive. The detail is quiet and grave.

options.text: the fading of the radio's music as the station's evening broadcast came to its end
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The phrase belongs to 'my mother's voice', and the radio is turned up, not fading.

refs.quote: my mother's voice going small, then smaller,

evidence_quotes: my mother's voice going small, then smaller,

items.stem: The speaker's statement "So don't think I've come here to accuse you" ([[r1]]) reveals a complexity in her attitude because she

options.text: disowns an accusation she has largely made, after admitting her own share in the silence
options.label: correct
options.why: The earlier stanzas charge the house with hearing and holding everything. Having just confessed that she turned up the radio, she takes back the charge, which shows both blame and guilt at work.

options.text: sincerely forgives the house, since she now believes that nothing wrong ever happened inside
options.label: reversal
options.why: She has just recalled the chair against the door and her mother's shrinking voice. She does not deny that wrong happened.

options.text: threatens the house with a harsher accusation that she plans to make before she leaves
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: No threat follows. She locks up and leaves quietly.

options.text: shifts the blame from her father onto the house, which she now sees as the true wrongdoer
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The line says the opposite: she is not accusing the house. The blame turns toward herself, not onto the house.

refs.quote: So don't think I've come here to accuse you.

evidence_quotes: But I was the one who turned the radio up.
So don't think I've come here to accuse you.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the function of the final line of the poem?

options.text: It recasts the speaker's composed departure as a learned evasion, linking it to the radio.
options.label: correct
options.why: Not turning around is called being 'raised better'. Yet what she was raised in was covering harm with noise, so her calm exit repeats the habit she confessed in the fifth stanza.

options.text: It resolves the poem's tension by showing that the speaker has fully healed and can move on.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The irony of 'raised better' leaves the tension unresolved. Her leaving looks like avoidance, not healing.

options.text: It introduces a religious theme that the earlier stanzas of the poem have not prepared for.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The allusion is not a new theme. It sums up the poem's concern with looking at, or away from, the past.

options.text: It reveals that the speaker's parents were strict about religion as well as about silence.
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: This reads 'raised better' as a literal report of religious training. The line is ironic, not a fact about the family's faith.

evidence_quotes: Lot's wife looked back. I was raised better than that.
I was the one who turned the radio up

items.stem: Across the poem, the radio ([[r1]]) and ([[r2]]) functions as a symbol of

options.text: noise used to drown out harm, and of the speaker's own part in keeping it unheard
options.label: correct
options.why: At first the radio is 'turned up to cover it'. After the volta it becomes the speaker's own act, so it stands for concealment and for her complicity in it.

options.text: the outside world, which offered the family a hopeful escape from its troubles at home
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The radio is used to cover what happens, not to escape it. No hope is attached to it.

options.text: the father's power over the household, since he alone controlled what the family heard
options.label: reversal
options.why: It is the speaker who 'knew the dial' and turned it up, so the father does not control the radio.

options.text: the speaker's love of music, which she associates with the happiest times in the house
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The 'loudest band' is chosen for volume, to cover the noise. It is not chosen out of love or connected with happiness.

refs.quote: the radio turned up to cover it
I was the one who turned the radio up

evidence_quotes: the radio turned up to cover it.
I knew which station had the loudest band.

items.stem: The contrast between the buyers' praise of "the quiet" ([[r1]]) and the earlier image of walls "so thick no neighbor ever heard" ([[r2]]) primarily serves to

options.text: show that the quality the buyers admire is the one that once hid the family's trouble
options.label: correct
options.why: The quiet the couple praises comes from the same thick walls that kept the violence unheard. 'They'll mean it as a compliment' marks the gap between what they know and what she knows.

options.text: suggest that the house has finally become peaceful now that the troubled family has left
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The house may be quiet now, but the poem's point is the continuity between this quiet and the earlier concealment, not a new peace.

options.text: reveal the speaker's envy of the young couple and of the happy family they will have there
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The speaker expresses no envy. Her remark about the couple is dry, not wistful.

options.text: criticize the buyers for being careless about the safety of the baby they bring with them
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The speaker does not blame the couple. Their ignorance is innocent, and the irony falls on the house and on her.

refs.quote: stand in your front room and praise the quiet
walls so thick no neighbor ever heard

evidence_quotes: will stand in your front room and praise the quiet.

items.stem: Which of the following claims about the poem is best supported by the text?

options.text: The speaker's account of the house gradually becomes an account of her own complicity.
options.label: correct
options.why: The poem moves from what the house 'heard' and 'held' to 'I was the one who turned the radio up', and ends with her own habit of not looking back.

options.text: The speaker sells the house chiefly to punish it for the violence it allowed to happen.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: No motive for the sale is given, and she explicitly says she has not come to accuse the house.

options.text: The poem suggests that all well-built houses in the town concealed similar family violence.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The poem concerns one house and one family. It makes no claim about other houses.

options.text: The speaker remembers the house with uncomplicated fondness despite its creaky old age.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Her memories include the barred door and her mother's shrinking voice, so her attitude is anything but uncomplicated fondness.

spec.premise: the speaker walks the length of a closed railway

set.title: Trackbed, Kell Valley Branch
set.headnote: The following poem is by the contemporary poet Isla Brennick. The speaker walks the route of a railway branch line that closed many years earlier.

blueprint.speaker: A woman in her mid-thirties, born the year a rural branch line was dismantled, the daughter of a former track worker
blueprint.addressee: Her father, once a ganger on the line, now in a wheelchair at a care home called Fairholme
blueprint.situation: At her father's request she walks the eleven miles of the closed Kell Valley branch, from Ashby Halt to Corran, carrying his flask and map, supposedly to check the track keys at Dunmore cutting, though the rails were lifted decades ago
blueprint.central_idea: The errand is not a test of the father's failing memory but a way of lending him the walk his body can no longer make; the daughter's planned lie that the keys are holding becomes a loving support, like the small wooden key that holds a rail in place.
blueprint.complexity: The poem first seems to show a confused old man sending his daughter on a pointless task. At the volta the speaker realizes he knew all along, since he pulled the last keys himself. Pity turns into an unspoken understanding. The closing lie is both untrue and faithful: a fiction both of them accept, described in the language of track-building so that the poem praises a deception without being sentimental about it.
blueprint.form_notes: Five free-verse stanzas of uneven length (5, 6, 7, 8, 7 lines). Plain, concrete diction with railway vocabulary (keys, sleepers, cutting, ganger). Enjambment carries the walk forward. The volta sits in the middle of the fourth stanza and is marked by a colon and a caesura. The final stanza is one long sentence that settles into the closing metaphor.
blueprint.setting: The cinder trackbed of a closed rural branch line, overgrown with cow parsley, passing mileposts, gardens built from old sleepers, and a damp stone cutting; present day, summer
blueprint.conflict: The gap between the father's errand and what is actually left of the line, and the speaker's choice between telling him the truth and telling him a kind lie

stanzas: "Walk it for me," you said, "the whole eleven,
Ashby Halt to Corran. And check the keys
at Dunmore cutting. They work loose in heat."
So here I am with your flask and your map,
folded so often the river has worn through.
The rails went for scrap the year I was born.
What's left is cinder laid across the fields
like a parting combed in a child's hair
the morning of a photograph. Cow parsley
up to my shoulder. A woman with a spaniel
nods as if I'd come to read the meter.
Milepost three. Milepost four, its numbers
rubbed bright by someone's thumb, or weather.
No sleepers either. They went for fences,
for raised beds, for the step outside the Drover's.
Of all the sleepers you are the last one
still on the line, in your chair at Fairholme,
brakes on, the television naming birds.
At Dunmore cutting there is nothing to tighten.
The walls sweat green. A wren goes off
like a dropped spanner, and the cold
comes up out of the stone, and I see it:
you knew. You pulled the last keys yourself
in nineteen eighty-three, with a bar and a curse.
What you have lost is not the map. It's the walk,
eleven miles, a sentence you can't finish.
So I finish it for you, at your pace,
the old one, a ganger's, eyes on the ground,
and tonight I'll tell you the keys are holding.
It's the kind of lie you taught me, the kind
a railway's made of: small, wooden, driven
hard into the gap to keep the heavy thing
from shifting while the weight goes over.

spec.premise: a grandfather's bench in the village square

set.title: The Bench in Vrana Square
set.headnote: The following poem is by an invented writer, set in a small river village some years after a war.

blueprint.speaker: An adult grandson, educated in the city, who left the village in forty-nine and has come back after his grandfather's burial
blueprint.addressee: His dead grandfather, addressed directly as 'Grandfather' and 'you'
blueprint.situation: A month after the grandfather's burial, the village council is about to remove his bench from the square to make room for a glass bus shelter. The speaker sits on the bench and remembers the old man's daily vigil, which the whole village believed was kept only for Pavel, the son taken away by trucks in forty-two.
blueprint.setting: A village square with a fountain, the eastern road and the western city road, around 1961
characters: Pavel, the grandfather's son, taken in forty-two
blueprint.central_idea: The grandson finds out that the vigil he scorned as a boy, which everyone took to be grief for a lost son, was also kept for him, the grandson who left and stopped writing. His adolescent shame turns into adult guilt.
blueprint.complexity: The poem is divided between public and private, past and present understanding. The village reveres the grandfather's grief and the boy despises his idleness, and both readings are partial. The worn west armrest shows a second, hidden waiting. So the speaker is both mourner and culprit, and the removal of the bench for a timetabled shelter sets the old man's open-ended faithfulness against a modern order the speaker himself chose.
blueprint.conflict: The speaker's guilt over his neglect against his earlier embarrassment, and the village's public story against the private evidence of the bench
blueprint.form_notes: Six unrhymed stanzas of plain, conversational free verse. Short declarative sentences and caesurae carry the confessions. Enjambment carries the memory and discovery. The poem turns in the fifth stanza at 'It is not at the fountain end' and closes on a three-line stanza ending in a stopped, confessional line.

devices.quote: a month after they moved you up the hill
devices.function: A euphemism for burial that sets the removal of the man beside the removal of his bench, with restrained grief.

devices.quote: glass on three sides, a timetable under glass
devices.function: A transparent, scheduled modern structure set against the grandfather's open-ended waiting.

devices.quote: Mornings you took the end beside the fountain
devices.function: Sets up the public, east-facing vigil for Pavel that the later afternoon detail complicates.

devices.quote: Like the old dog on the dung heap at Ithaca
devices.function: Recalls Odysseus's faithful dog, who waited twenty years and knew his master on his return. It frames the grandfather's humble loyalty, which no returning figure ever rewards.

devices.quote: lowered their voices, as if you were a church
devices.function: Shows the villagers' reverent but distant treatment of the old man's grief.

devices.quote: I was ashamed of you. I was fourteen.
devices.function: The mid-line stop isolates a blunt confession and gives his age as context, not excuse.

devices.quote: or lied about the war over plum brandy
devices.function: 'Lied' shows that the boy preferred a comfortable performance to honest, silent grief.

devices.quote: not one who sat all day like a stopped clock
devices.function: The boy's dismissive view of the grandfather as useless. It is ironic, because the old man was in fact keeping close time for the bus.

devices.quote: to the polytechnic and the city's
devices.function: The line runs on into 'brick and neon', pulling the reader along with the speaker's departure.

devices.quote: then at Christmas, then I meant to write.
devices.function: The dwindling series records neglect by easy stages, ending in an intention instead of an act.

devices.quote: It is not at the fountain end. It is
devices.function: Turns from memory to discovery and overturns the village's story of the vigil.

devices.quote: goes looking for the place your hand wore smooth
devices.function: The worn place on the bench stands for the hidden direction of the grandfather's devotion.

devices.quote: you slid sideways down the slats
devices.function: The soft repeated s sounds suggest the quiet, private movement toward the city side.

devices.quote: Twelve years I let you think the road was slow.
devices.function: The old man blamed the road, but the real delay was the speaker's. The last line turns the poem into a confession.

shifts.from: a description of the bench and the village's reverence
shifts.to: the speaker's blunt confession of his adolescent shame

provenance.note: Original poem in a mid-twentieth-century plain-spoken free-verse manner; invented author, village and characters.

stanzas: They are moving your bench on Thursday, Grandfather,
a month after they moved you up the hill,
to make room for a shelter the council voted,
glass on three sides, a timetable under glass.
Today it still stands where you bolted it down
the spring the river took the mill, its slats
gone gray as a mule's muzzle, one short leg
shimmed with a folded jack of clubs.
The whole square knew what you were doing there.
Mornings you took the end beside the fountain
and turned your hat-brim to the eastern road
the trucks had carried Pavel down in forty-two.
Like the old dog on the dung heap at Ithaca
who lived to know his master's step, you waited,
and the women crossing with their bread
lowered their voices, as if you were a church.
I was ashamed of you. I was fourteen.
I wanted a grandfather who mended nets
or lied about the war over plum brandy,
not one who sat all day like a stopped clock
and asked the postman, every noon, the same
two words, and thanked him for the answer.
In forty-nine I took the western bus
to the polytechnic and the city's
brick and neon, and I wrote at Easter,
then at Christmas, then I meant to write.
You never asked me why. You asked the postman.
Now I sit where you sat, and my hand
goes looking for the place your hand wore smooth.
It is not at the fountain end. It is
the other arm, rubbed pale as soap, the arm
that faces west, down the city road.
Afternoons, then, when the square had stopped
watching, you slid sideways down the slats to me.
On Thursday they will truck it to the depot.
The new bus will halt where your boots halted.
Twelve years I let you think the road was slow.

spec.premise: a boy learning to whistle a song his father never finished

set.title: The Upper Gate
set.headnote: The following poem is a nineteenth-century-style piece by an invented poet. The speaker lives beside a canal lock.

blueprint.speaker: Tom's widow, the mother of the boy, at a canal lock-keeper's house
blueprint.addressee: Her dead husband, Tom, the former lock-keeper
blueprint.situation: On an evening after tea, the widow watches her son stand on the lock-beam and whistle his dead father's tune. He gets as far as Tom always went, stops, and then makes up his own ending, which the boat drivers carry off along the towpath. In the last stanza she reveals that Tom never finished the tune because she used to sing its ending, and she chooses not to sing it now.
blueprint.central_idea: Loving the dead can mean holding back what they left you, so that the living can make something of their own. The widow's silence keeps the past in check, as a lock gate holds back water.
blueprint.complexity: Her silence is both possessive and generous. She keeps the true ending, the last private bond of her marriage, for herself, and in doing so she gives her son the freedom to finish the song his own way. The town will credit the boy with an ending that replaces hers, so her act is fidelity and self-erasure at once. Whether this is grief or love, she presents it without sentiment.
blueprint.form_notes: Five stanzas of loose blank verse, in the manner of a nineteenth-century domestic dramatic monologue. The first four stanzas flow into each other through enjambed stanza breaks (each of the first three ends on a comma or semicolon), which mimics the tune running on. The final stanza turns with a second apostrophe to Tom and ends on short, stopped sentences.

devices.function: Speaking to the dead husband frames the whole poem as a private report to him, which sets up the confession at the end.

devices.quote: like one who blows the chaff from off his palm
devices.function: The boy's whistling posture becomes a farm-like act of sifting and testing to see what is left, and the image ties him to his father's gesture.

devices.quote: and then the dry step in it where you'd stop
devices.function: The pause in the music is pictured as a dry step in a lock chamber, so the gap in the tune belongs to the world of the canal.

devices.quote: lifts its brown shoulder, waiting, as it waited
devices.function: The water in the lock seems to wait for the rest of the tune as it once waited on Tom's work, so the scene itself is held in suspense.

devices.quote: the heron on the far bank holds one foot
devices.function: A precise image of stillness that adds to the hush at the place where the tune stops.

devices.quote: No Orpheus, he; he cannot whistle you
devices.function: The singer of myth who tried to bring his wife back from the dead with song, and lost her by looking back. The speaker admits song cannot restore Tom and hints that she would not have her son look backward.

devices.quote: I did not call to him. I had my reasons.
devices.function: Hints at what she is holding back, which the final stanza reveals.

devices.quote: He tries an ending. It is wrong. He tries
devices.function: Breaking the line into short sentences records each separate attempt with close, plain attention.

devices.quote: another, sharper, like a boy's new knife,
devices.function: The boy's own ending is fresh and cutting, a young person's tool, unlike the father's habits.

devices.quote: and the drivers drag it down the towpath with them,

devices.quote: his ending on your beginning, all the way
devices.function: Puts son and father together in one song, joined but different.

devices.quote: They will call it his by Sunday.
devices.function: The town will credit the boy, unaware that a true ending exists and that the speaker is keeping it.

devices.quote: Tom, it was never for the want of notes

devices.quote: I keep it shut, the way you kept the gate

blueprint.setting: A canal lock and lock-keeper's cottage in an invented English canal town, mid-nineteenth century, at evening after tea; the towpath runs toward Coldmere Locks, and Tom is buried in Wendlecote churchyard.
characters: the coal-boat drivers on the towpath
blueprint.conflict: The widow's wish to keep the last private part of her marriage, set against her son's need to finish the song as his own; also memory against continuation.

provenance.note: Original poem written for practice use, in a nineteenth-century manner; author and places are invented.

stanzas: Tom, he has got your tune as far as you.
He stands upon the lock-beam after tea
and screws his mouth up sideways, as you did,
like one who blows the chaff from off his palm
to see what grain is left there; and it comes,
the first part clean, the second bending down,
and then the dry step in it where you'd stop
to knock your pipe out on the windlass post.
He stops there too. The water in the chamber
lifts its brown shoulder, waiting, as it waited
for every boat you ever let go down;
the heron on the far bank holds one foot.
I did not call to him. I had my reasons.
No Orpheus, he; he cannot whistle you
up out of Wendlecote churchyard with a tune,
and I would not have had him looking back.
He tries an ending. It is wrong. He tries
another, sharper, like a boy's new knife,
and that one holds. He whistles it again,
pleased with himself, again, until the coal-boats hear,
and the drivers drag it down the towpath with them,
his ending on your beginning, all the way
to Coldmere Locks, as if it had been so
since Adam. They will call it his by Sunday.
Tom, it was never for the want of notes
you stopped. You stopped because the rest was mine:
you whistled to the turn, and I sang down
the falling part across the drying-yard,
your shirts in my two arms. I have it still.
I keep it shut, the way you kept the gate
against the press of all the upper water,
and let his run downstream. I do not sing.

spec.premise: a persona poem spoken by a seed in a vault

set.title: Accession 4471-B
set.headnote: The following poem is by the contemporary poet Maren Oduya. The speaker is a seed held in long-term frozen storage.

blueprint.speaker: A single speckled bean, catalogued as an accession in a frozen seed repository inside a northern mountain, donated years ago by a farmer named Teodor Halas
blueprint.addressee: No one at first (a general listener); in the final stanza the seed turns and addresses the dead farmer Teodor directly
blueprint.situation: Nine years into cold storage, the seed describes its nested enclosure, the twice-yearly inspection by a technician named Dagny, and its memory of the farmer who sealed its envelope. It then admits what its release would require.
blueprint.central_idea: Being preserved is not the same as living. The vault keeps the seed safe by keeping it from doing what it was made for, so its natural longing to grow can only come true through the disasters the vault exists to guard against.
blueprint.complexity: The seed is grateful and loyal (to Teodor, even to the cold 'kindness'), yet it resents a safety that feels like burial. Its desire to be needed is innocent in itself but turns into a guilty wish for catastrophe. It becomes 'a prayer that should not be answered,' and the final 'crack' means both sprouting and breaking down.
blueprint.form_notes: Free verse, 32 lines in five stanzas of uneven length. Long conversational lines are broken by enjambment, which mimics nesting and waiting (envelope inside box inside mountain). The volta comes at the opening of the fifth stanza with 'But.' The last line rests on a pun.
blueprint.setting: A contemporary seed repository cut into a mountain, kept at minus eighteen degrees, with aisles of shelves and lights that come on twice a year
characters: Teodor Halas, the farmer who donated the beans, now dead
blueprint.conflict: The seed's drive to split and grow versus its purpose as an emergency reserve that is only used if the world above fails

devices.quote: They tell me minus eighteen is a kindness.
devices.function: The seed repeats the official view that freezing is care while quietly doubting it, which sets up the gap between safety and life.

devices.quote: inside a box inside a mountain
devices.function: The repeated 'inside' piles up layers of enclosure and isolation.

devices.quote: inside a box inside a mountain
devices.function: The line runs on into 'for nine years,' so the enclosure stretches into time as well as space.

devices.quote: in a coat as thick as a mattress
devices.function: The bulky, domestic comparison makes the cold felt and makes Dagny seem padded off from the seeds.

devices.quote: reading the shelves like a teacher calling roll
devices.function: Compares the inspection to taking attendance 'in a school where nobody answers,' which stresses the seeds' silence and how routine and impersonal the check is.

devices.quote: salt and pipe smoke, a man who talked to rows
devices.function: Sensory detail of taste and smell brings up the warm, living human world the seed came from, in contrast to the vault's cold.

devices.quote: good in poor ground. Do not let them dry out.
devices.function: The farmer's praise of the bean's hardiness looks ahead to the 'poor ground' of drought and ruin in which the seed would finally be needed.

devices.quote: as if they might talk back. He has died since.
devices.function: The full stop in mid-line sets the news of Teodor's death abruptly against the memory of his liveliness.

devices.quote: who ate six of our red cousins in the underworld
devices.function: Points to the myth of the girl who ate pomegranate seeds in the underworld and had to stay below part of each year. It frames the vault as an underworld, but one with no spring release.

devices.quote: At least they let her up for spring.
devices.function: Sets the girl's seasonal return against the seed's open-ended confinement.

devices.quote: The mountain is patient. It has never wanted
devices.function: Giving the mountain patience and a lack of desire makes it a foil to the seed's wanting and shows that the vault's safety is indifferent.

devices.quote: But I was made for one thing, which is splitting.
devices.function: Turns from description and memory to confession of the seed's purpose and desire.

devices.quote: So I am a prayer
devices.function: The seed sees itself as a prayer that should not be answered, a paradox: its fulfillment would mean disaster.

devices.quote: Forgive me, Teodor.
devices.function: The direct address to the dead farmer turns the seed's desire into a guilty confession to the person who cared for it.

devices.quote: Some nights I want it so badly I almost crack.
devices.function: 'Crack' means both germinating (a seed splitting open) and breaking down under strain, which joins longing and distress in one word.

shifts.quote: Down here I think about the girl
shifts.from: concrete memory of the farmer
shifts.to: mythic reflection on confinement

shifts.quote: But I was made for one thing, which is splitting.
shifts.from: patient, wry description of being stored
shifts.to: urgent, guilty confession of desire for release

provenance.note: Original persona poem written for practice use; poet and all names invented.

stanzas: They tell me minus eighteen is a kindness.
I am a speckled bean from Teodor Halas's
upper field, the one that floods in April,
and I have slept inside a foil envelope
inside a box inside a mountain
for nine years, which is nothing, which is a breath.
Twice a year the light comes on. Dagny walks
the aisles in a coat as thick as a mattress,
reading the shelves like a teacher calling roll
in a school where nobody answers,
and goes out humming, and the dark shuts behind her.
Teodor wrote on our envelope in pencil:
good in poor ground. Do not let them dry out.
He licked the flap. I can still taste him,
salt and pipe smoke, a man who talked to rows
as if they might talk back. He has died since.
I know it the way we know a frost, without being told.
Down here I think about the girl
who ate six of our red cousins in the underworld
and had to stay below for half of every year.
At least they let her up for spring.
The mountain is patient. It has never wanted
anything, and it holds us the way a bank
holds a coin: to be worth something, never spent.
But I was made for one thing, which is splitting.
I practice it in my sleep. And what would open
the door for good is fire, or a war,
or the long drought they name in meetings,
the world above gone wrong enough
that someone needs me. So I am a prayer
that should not be answered. Forgive me, Teodor.
Some nights I want it so badly I almost crack.

items.stem: Which of the following statements is the most defensible thesis about the poem as a whole?

options.text: Through a stored seed's voice, the poem shows that being saved keeps the seed from living, so its wish to grow becomes a guilty wish for catastrophe.
options.label: correct
options.why: The poem moves from the doubted 'kindness' of cold storage to the admission that only 'fire, or a war, or the long drought' would free the seed, which makes it 'a prayer / that should not be answered.'

options.text: Through a stored seed's voice, the poem argues that every human effort to protect the natural world eventually harms the very living things it protects.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The poem looks at one seed's divided feelings about one vault. It makes no general claim about all conservation, and the seed itself is not shown to be harmed.

options.text: Through a stored seed's voice, the poem celebrates the vault as a calm and lasting refuge where the seed is content to wait out the troubles above.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The seed is not content. It says it was 'made for one thing, which is splitting' and wants release 'so badly I almost crack.'

options.text: Through a stored seed's voice, the poem mourns a dead farmer whose pencil note and sealed envelope are now the only traces of his life that survive.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Teodor's death is one element, but the poem's central tension is the seed's conflict between preservation and growth, not grief for the farmer.

evidence_quotes: They tell me minus eighteen is a kindness.
that someone needs me. So I am a prayer
Some nights I want it so badly I almost crack.

items.stem: Taken together with the final stanza, Teodor's note ([[r1]]) best supports which of the following claims?

options.text: The note's praise of the bean's hardiness quietly anticipates the hard times in which the seed would finally be needed.
options.label: correct
options.why: 'Good in poor ground' looks ahead to the 'long drought' and the 'world above gone wrong' that the final stanza names as the only conditions under which the seed would be planted.

options.text: The note shows that Teodor distrusted the vault's staff and fully expected them to neglect the beans he had donated.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing suggests distrust. The instruction reads as ordinary care, and Dagny is never shown neglecting anything.

options.text: The note shows that dryness, rather than the cold of the mountain, is the main danger the seed faces in storage.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: This takes 'dry out' as the poem's main concern. The final stanza places the real tension in the seed's longing and in the disasters above, not in storage conditions.

options.text: The note reveals that Teodor's land was so poor that beans were the only crop he could ever manage to grow.
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: The field is described only as one 'that floods in April.' The note praises the bean's toughness and says nothing about Teodor's farm being barren.

options.text: wry doubt about an official account of its care, which it repeats without fully accepting

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the function of the final line ([[r1]])?

spec.premise: the speaker counting trains from a rented room

set.title: Room Above the Coal Merchant's
set.headnote: The following poem is by an invented writer of the early twentieth century. The speaker lodges in a rented room beside a railway line.

blueprint.speaker: Miss Orrin, an unmarried woman lodging in a rented room above a coal merchant's near a railway line, shortly after a war in which her brother left by train
blueprint.addressee: No direct addressee; a private reckoning overheard by the reader, with the landlady Mrs. Pruett present in report and speech
blueprint.situation: From her window the speaker keeps a pencil tally of every passing train on the wallpaper. Her landlady brings water and gently teases her. Midway the speaker recalls her brother leaving on the six-ten one March, the one train she did not count; she now keeps an expired return ticket in her Bible and has counted four hundred and eleven trains.
blueprint.central_idea: Counting the trains looks like waiting to leave, but it is really a ritual of staying: a belated bookkeeping for the one departure she failed to mark, and a way of confirming that she herself remains.
blueprint.complexity: The speaker's tally is both devotion and evasion. It answers guilt over her brother's unmarked departure, yet it also lets her avoid the journey her ticket promises. The landlady reads her as someone about to go; the poem reveals she is both prisoner and warder of her own room. Precision becomes a form of grief, and departure-counting becomes proof of not departing.
blueprint.form_notes: Thirty-one lines in five unrhymed stanzas of loose blank verse. Three six-line stanzas of observation, a four-line stanza of memory that acts as the volta, and a longer final stanza that ends on a truncated four-word line. Enjambment carries the tally across lines; caesuras mark the clipped, factual voice.
blueprint.setting: A rented room above a coal merchant's on a street beside a rail line in an invented English-style junction town, around 1920; trains run to Harle and over the bridge at Corran.
characters: the speaker's brother, who left on the six-ten in March
blueprint.conflict: Internal: the speaker's wish to leave, or to have marked her brother's leaving, against her habit of staying and recording.

devices.quote: goes by like a drawer pulled open in the dark
devices.function: Domesticates the train as a brief glimpse offered and withdrawn, introducing the poem's pattern of things briefly opened and then shut.

devices.quote: like fences round a field where nothing grows
devices.function: Makes the tally marks enclosures around barrenness, hinting that the record guards an emptiness.

devices.quote: what all the little gates are for
devices.function: Turns the barred tally fives into gates, objects of passage that here let nothing through.

devices.quote: I did not know I was to keep the books.
devices.function: Presents counting as accounting, suggesting a debt owed for the brother's unmarked departure.

devices.quote: rails that talk in their sleep
devices.function: Gives the night line a restless, human inner life that mirrors the speaker's sleeplessness.

devices.quote: Four hundred and eleven, says the wall.
devices.function: Lets the wall announce the total, as if the record now speaks with more authority than the speaker.

devices.quote: Cattle, coal, and once a car
devices.function: The hard c sounds give the inventory of freight a clipped, ledger-like rhythm.

devices.quote: I make a mark for it
devices.function: Carries the act of marking over the line break onto the wallpaper, enacting the continuing tally.

devices.quote: I count the trains. The nine-fourteen to Harle
devices.function: The mid-line stop gives the voice its flat, factual restraint.

devices.quote: Miss Orrin, you'll wear that window thin.
devices.function: The landlady's kindly hyperbole names the speaker and shows how an outsider reads her watching.

devices.quote: Harle and back, third class, its date gone by.
devices.function: The expired return ticket stands for a journey intended and never taken.

devices.quote: Mrs. Pruett thinks I mean to go.
devices.function: The landlady takes the counting for readiness to leave, when it is a ritual of staying.

devices.quote: My brother went from here.
devices.function: Turns the poem from present observation to the memory that explains the counting.

devices.quote: bound for some parlor I will never sit in
devices.function: Sets even freight moving toward a life against the speaker's fixed room.

devices.quote: not for the ones who leave, but to be sure
devices.function: Counting departures becomes a way of confirming that she stays.

devices.quote: the long complaint
devices.function: Gives the train's sound the connotation of grievance.

devices.quote: you'll wear that window thin
devices.function: The window recurs as the frame of watching and of the brother's departure.

shifts.quote: My brother went from here.
shifts.from: detached present-tense cataloguing of trains and freight
shifts.to: a compressed, painful memory of the brother's departure

shifts.to: rueful self-assessment and the revelation that the counting is a way of staying

provenance.note: Original poem written for practice materials in an early twentieth-century manner; author and places invented.

stanzas: From the rented room above the coal merchant's
I count the trains. The nine-fourteen to Harle
goes by like a drawer pulled open in the dark
and shut again. I make a mark for it
in pencil on the wallpaper, by the bed,
where the roses have gone brown as tea.
Mrs. Pruett, bringing up the jug,
says, "Miss Orrin, you'll wear that window thin."
She means it kindly. She sets the water down
and does not ask what all the little gates are for,
the fives I bar across with one long stroke
like fences round a field where nothing grows.

with one piano roped beneath a sheet,
bound for some parlor I will never sit in.
The night ones I count by ear: the long complaint
of the up-line, rails that talk in their sleep,
the bridge at Corran taking each in its teeth.
My brother went from here. The six-ten, March,
the window down, his cap held out, and then
the window empty. That one I did not count.
I did not know I was to keep the books.
Now I am thorough. Now I keep a ticket
folded in the Bible on the washstand,
Harle and back, third class, its date gone by.
Mrs. Pruett thinks I mean to go.
Four hundred and eleven, says the wall.
Not one of them has taken me. I count
the way a warder counts the cells at night,
not for the ones who leave, but to be sure
that I am here.

spec.premise: a ferry operator and a passenger who rides without a destination

set.title: The Harlan Narrows Crossing
set.headnote: The following passage is from a short story by Orrin Delacourt, set at a river crossing in the early 1950s.

characters: Walt Ostrander, narrator, operator of a cable ferry since 1931
Mrs. Lorne, a woman who rides the ferry back and forth every Sunday without getting off
Lucille, who keeps the ticket booth and passes on gossip
blueprint.setting: The Harlan Narrows cable ferry between Pell's Landing and Cutbank, a river crossing, October 1952 to March 1953
blueprint.situation: A woman whose husband has left town rides the ferry back and forth every Sunday all winter. The operator insists he does not care, but he keeps changing small habits for her. In March she gets off for good with a suitcase.
blueprint.conflict: The narrator's claimed indifference against his growing, unadmitted attention to Mrs. Lorne. Underneath that is the conflict between his fixed, repeating life and the possibility of leaving it, which she takes and he does not.
blueprint.central_idea: Going back and forth can be a way of putting off a decision. The woman who seems aimless uses it to make up her mind and then leaves. The man who carries other people to where they are going turns out to be the one with no destination.
blueprint.complexity: The narrator's denials ('it did not trouble me,' 'There was no call to') show the feeling they deny. The needle metaphor works both as a defense of steady work and as an admission of a life that never finishes anything. Mrs. Lorne's question about how many crossings he has made exposes his lie and suggests that she sees in him the stalled condition she is escaping. The ending puts his old routines back in place, but the reader now sees them as confinement.

devices.quote: like a woman feeling for the banister in the dark
devices.function: Compares the ferry to a cautious, groping woman. This anticipates Mrs. Lorne and makes the fixed course look careful but blind.

devices.quote: the Corley is a needle and the river is a hem
devices.function: The ferry is a needle sewing a hem that never gets finished. It describes work that repeats without ever completing anything, and the narrator offers it as a self-justification.

devices.quote: The ramp came down with its usual iron complaint
devices.function: Gives the machinery a voice of routine grumbling at the moment the routine breaks.

devices.quote: It goes in and comes out. It goes in
devices.function: The repeated sentence imitates the endless back-and-forth of the crossings.

devices.quote: I have never once wondered where anybody was going
devices.function: His claim of incuriosity is undercut by everything he goes on to notice. The ending turns it back on him.

devices.quote: the light on the water had gone the color of weak tea
devices.function: Marks the fading of a long afternoon of repeated crossings and sets a dim, diluted mood.

devices.quote: I did take to wiping down the upstream rail
devices.function: The rail and the thermos are small habits he changes for her and keeps up after she is gone. They show the attachment he will not name.

devices.quote: I will say plainly that it did not trouble me
devices.function: His flat denial calls attention to the feeling it is meant to hide.

devices.quote: On the last Sunday in March she came aboard
devices.function: Moves from describing the habitual Sundays to a single decisive day.

devices.quote: I took them where they were going
devices.function: The other passengers have destinations and he has none. This recasts who in the story is really aimless.

devices.quote: put the thermos back under the bench where it belongs
devices.function: Putting the thermos back stands for his retreat into the old order.

blueprint.speaker: Walt Ostrander, first-person, looking back on the winter. He is laconic and defensive, and he hides his feelings even from himself.
blueprint.form_notes: Seven paragraphs. Paragraph one sets out the fixed course and the narrator's creed. The last paragraph returns to the same course with the meaning reversed. Dialogue is kept terse.
blueprint.addressee: An implied general listener, one of the 'people who ask'

provenance.note: Original passage written for practice use.

stanzas: The Harlan Narrows ferry runs on a cable, which is
the first thing I tell people who ask whether it ever
gets lost. It cannot get lost. Seven hundred yards of
greased wire lie along the bottom from Pell's Landing to
Cutbank, and the Ida Corley pulls herself along it like
a woman feeling for the banister in the dark. Eleven
minutes each way. I have run her since the spring of
1931, and in that time I have never once wondered where
anybody was going. Wondering is for people on the bank.
Mrs. Lorne began in October of 1952. She paid her
fifteen cents at Pell's, went to the upstream rail, and
stood there with her pocketbook held against her stomach
in both hands. At Cutbank the trucks rolled off and the
feed-store man rolled off and she did not. She paid
again. I took the money because it was money. By the
fourth crossing the light on the water had gone the
color of weak tea, and she was still at the rail, and I
had stopped pretending to look at the gauge.
'You'll want to get off one side or the other,' I
told her, round about the sixth trip. 'We tie up at
seven.' 'I know when you tie up. It's on the sign.'
'There's nothing at Cutbank but the feed store and a
church with no bell.' 'I've been to Cutbank,' she said,
the way you'd say you'd been to the dentist. Then she
asked how many times I had crossed, all told, and I said
I had no idea, which was a lie. I had worked it out one
winter on the back of a tide table, and it came to
something over ninety thousand.
She came every Sunday after that, and I will say
plainly that it did not trouble me. A passenger is a
passenger. I did take to wiping down the upstream rail
before the first run, but that was on account of the
gulls, and if I kept the thermos of coffee on the bench
instead of under it, that was only where it was
handiest. I noticed her shoes were the same brown pair
every week, resoled once in January. I noticed she never
looked toward either landing, only at the water going
under, as if she were reading it.
Lucille, who keeps the ticket booth at Pell's, said
the woman was not right. Lucille said Mr. Lorne had gone
to Detroit in the summer and sent back a postcard of a
hotel. I said that was nobody's business. The way I see
it, the Corley is a needle and the river is a hem that
never gets finished, and a needle has no opinion about
the cloth. It goes in and comes out. It goes in and
comes out. A man could do worse than be a needle.
On the last Sunday in March she came aboard with a
suitcase, a tan cardboard one with a strap buckled in
the wrong hole. She set it by the rail and stood beside
it and we crossed, and at Cutbank she picked it up. The
ramp came down with its usual iron complaint. She
stopped on the second plank. 'I wanted to see if it got
easier, going over and over,' she said. 'It doesn't. It
only gets the same.' She looked at me then, straight on,
the first time since October. 'How many did you say, Mr.
Ostrander?' 'I didn't say.' 'No,' she said. 'You
didn't.'
She went up the road past the feed store toward
where the county bus stops, and I hauled the ramp and
took the Corley back to Pell's with nobody aboard,
eleven minutes, the wire coming up dripping over the
sheave and going down again behind. I did not watch the
Cutbank side. There was no call to. When we tied up I
wiped the upstream rail, out of habit, and put the
thermos back under the bench where it belongs, and on
Monday the trucks came the same as always and I took
them where they were going.

spec.premise: an old fisherman refuses the harbour master's offer of a pension

set.title: The Patience
set.headnote: The following passage is from a story by an invented writer, set in a northern English fishing harbour in the nineteenth century.

characters: Mr. Pell, the narrator, once a seventeen-year-old harbour clerk, now looking back
Mr. Harrowby, the harbour master, a narrow, exact man
Josiah Venn, an old fisherman who owns the coble Patience
blueprint.setting: The harbour and harbour office of Skelwick, a small northern fishing town, in the mid-nineteenth century; later the kitchen of the Harrowby house
blueprint.situation: Harrowby offers Venn a Trust pension on condition that his rotten boat be broken up; Venn refuses. Months later the narrator finds that Harrowby secretly buys Venn's small catch every week at four times its price.
blueprint.conflict: Venn's pride and need to keep working against the plain fact of his age and poverty; the young narrator's ledger-minded judgment against a kindness that does not show in any ledger
blueprint.central_idea: Real charity sometimes has to be hidden so that it does not shame the person who gets it. A mind that trusts only what can be written down will misread both pride and kindness.
blueprint.complexity: Harrowby looks cold, but he is careful. He repeats the offer each year so that Venn can refuse it, while he keeps Venn going through the fish purchases. The retrospective narrator shows how his younger self misjudged Harrowby and gently mocks him for it. The ending raises the question of whether Venn's independence is real or a fiction kept up by others, and it suggests the fiction is a gift.

devices.function: Shows the stranded boats as spent, resigned working creatures, which mirrors Venn's position

devices.quote: less a boat than a long black scab
devices.function: Makes the Patience look like a wound that has been patched over and over, worn but still hanging on

devices.quote: as if the words were tolls
devices.function: Harrowby's reading sounds official and transactional and hides any feeling

devices.quote: the floor took his weight with a complaint
devices.function: The office itself seems to register Venn's age and heaviness

devices.quote: all of them were unsigned
devices.function: Hints that the offer is a yearly ritual, which the ending confirms

devices.quote: It is only arithmetic.
devices.function: Harrowby uses cold language to hide a generosity that has nothing to do with arithmetic

devices.quote: weighing out three small codling on the brass scale
devices.function: Measuring stands for the ledger mind; here it serves a hidden overpayment, so value goes beyond measure

devices.quote: kept only by being left out
devices.function: The final insight: some accounts are honoured only by not being recorded

devices.quote: It was not until the autumn
devices.function: Moves from indignant judgment to a humbled discovery

shifts.quote: It was not until the autumn
shifts.from: the young clerk's confident condemnation of Harrowby
shifts.to: discovery of Harrowby's secret kindness and the narrator's chastened understanding

blueprint.speaker: Pell, an older man recalling his youth as a clerk
blueprint.form_notes: Seven paragraphs of retrospective first-person prose. The reveal is held back until the final paragraph.

stanzas: In the spring of the year the Trust put up its new
lamp on the north pier, Mr. Harrowby sent me down to the
shingle to fetch Josiah Venn. I was then seventeen. I
kept the harbour books, and I believed that anything
which could be entered in a ledger could be understood.
The tide was out, and the boats lay on their sides
in the mud like cattle that had given up. Venn's coble,
the Patience, was the oldest of them. Her strakes had
been tarred so often that she seemed less a boat than a
long black scab upon the harbour. He was sitting in her,
mending a net that had no fish in it to keep.
The harbour office smelt of lamp oil and wet wool.
Mr. Harrowby did not rise. He was a narrow, exact man
who wound his watch at noon whether it wanted winding or
not, and he read the paper aloud to Venn as if the words
were tolls: seven shillings weekly from the Trust's
benevolent fund, for the remainder of his natural life,
on condition that the coble Patience be surrendered and
broken up, she being a hazard to navigation.
'Broken up,' Venn said. 'For a hazard.' 'For
firewood, very likely,' said Mr. Harrowby. 'The
almshouse could use her.' Venn turned his cap in his
hands, once round, as a man turns a coin he suspects.
'I've a catch most days.' 'You have a catch,' Mr.
Harrowby agreed, 'most days.' Then he looked at me, and
I wrote nothing, because there was nothing in his voice
that a pen could take hold of.
'Then I'll keep to it,' said Venn. 'The Trust may
keep its shillings for a man as is done.' He stood, and
the floor took his weight with a complaint, and he went
out into the light. Through the window I watched him go
down the slip, his shoulders working as though he were
already at the oars.
I said, I am afraid with some heat, that it was a
cruelty to put such a choice to an old man, and that the
Trust might have let him keep his boat and his shillings
both. Mr. Harrowby blotted the paper and laid it in the
drawer with the others. There were, I saw, a good many
others, and all of them were unsigned. 'The Trust is not
unkind, Mr. Pell,' he said. 'It is only arithmetic.' I
thought him then the coldest man in Skelwick, and I
entered as much in my private book that evening, in a
hand I was proud of.
It was not until the autumn, when I was sent to the
Harrowby house with the quarter's accounts, that I came
in by the kitchen door and found the housekeeper
weighing out three small codling on the brass scale.
They were Venn's; I knew the tarred twine he threaded
through their gills. She paid the boy who had brought
them a shilling and sixpence, which was four times what
they would fetch on the quay. She wrote the sum not in
the household book but on a slip, which she pinned
behind the clock. 'The master's orders,' she said,
seeing my face. 'Every Friday. He says the Trust's offer
is made each spring so that Venn may have the pleasure
of refusing it.' I went home and did not open my private
book. There are figures, I have since learned, that are
kept only by being left out.

spec.premise: a translator is asked to read a dying man's letter aloud

set.title: Canon One
set.headnote: The following passage is from a contemporary short story. The narrator works as a professional interpreter.

characters: The narrator, a professional Portuguese medical and legal interpreter, unnamed
Aurelio Furtado, a dying man from the Azores-like islands, in hospice
Dana, his daughter, about fifty, raised in English
blueprint.setting: Room 14 at Saint Brendan's hospice in Halsey County, a coastal harbor town, on a snowy Tuesday in winter, present day
blueprint.situation: The interpreter is called to read aloud, in English, a letter Aurelio wrote in Portuguese to the daughter he left decades ago. When she reaches his blunt explanation for leaving, she secretly rewrites it as an apology.
blueprint.speaker: First-person narrator, the interpreter, telling the story afterward
blueprint.conflict: Internal: her professional canon of faithful rendering against the wish to spare Dana. External and unspoken: the gap between father and daughter, kept in place by language.
blueprint.central_idea: An act of interpretation can be both mercy and betrayal. The reconciliation the room witnesses is partly the interpreter's own composition, and its rightness cannot be settled.
blueprint.complexity: The narrator breaks the rule she is proud of, and the break produces the first tenderness between father and daughter. Aurelio's 'That is not what I wrote' exposes the change, and her second mistranslation compounds it. His closed eyes keep his judgment, anger or relief, out of reach. A strong essay would discuss the cold imagery as a fragile thaw, the plow as an emblem of erasure, the card as a motif of conscience, and the ironic last line.

devices.quote: like plates left overnight in a sink
devices.function: Makes the iced trawlers look stalled and neglected, a domestic image that anticipates the 'kitchen' of the letter.

devices.quote: a blanket the color of weak tea
devices.function: Gives the sickroom a faded, diluted look that matches the man's diminished state.

devices.quote: He made sure of that.
devices.function: Points to the resentment the letter will touch and to language as the barrier between them.

devices.quote: let them out with a small complaint
devices.function: Turns the oxygen machine into a weary worker, stressing how laboriously his life is being prolonged.

devices.quote: Faithfully, the card said.
devices.function: The laminated ethics card comes back as the narrator's conscience, from its introduction to the last paragraph.

devices.quote: Without omission. Without distortion.
devices.function: Clipped fragments act out her deliberation as she recites the rule to herself.

devices.quote: scraping it bare, scraping it bare
devices.function: The plow's repeated erasing mirrors the temptation to wipe out the written sentence.

devices.quote: a plow went back and forth across the same stretch
devices.function: The plow stands for erasure and for clearing a path, both of which her rewriting does.

devices.quote: I went because I was afraid
devices.function: Set against 'I went because I was happy with Lurdes,' it shows the gap between what was written and what is heard.

devices.quote: Dana's mouth did something it had not decided to do.
devices.function: Shows emotion breaking through without naming it.

devices.quote: My voice was a borrowed coat
devices.function: Casts her voice as something on loan from Aurelio that she returns altered, which admits her change.

devices.quote: That is not what I wrote.
devices.function: Aurelio's only words reveal that he understood, and they recast the whole reading.

devices.quote: He says I read it well
devices.function: A second mistranslation that sounds like praise covers both her betrayals.

shifts.quote: I went because I was afraid
shifts.from: faithful rendering of the letter
shifts.to: the narrator's silent invention

shifts.quote: When I finished, Mr. Furtado's eyes were open.
shifts.from: the reading as a private act between narrator and daughter
shifts.to: exposure before the father, who has understood

blueprint.form_notes: Eight paragraphs of first-person retrospective narration. The decision to alter the letter happens in the break between the fifth and sixth paragraphs.

provenance.note: Original short story written for practice-exam use.

stanzas: The hospice called the agency at eleven on a
Tuesday, and the agency called me, because I am the only
Portuguese interpreter in Halsey County who will drive
in snow. Room 14 at Saint Brendan's faced the parking
lot and, past it, the gray chop of the harbor, where the
trawlers sat frozen to their moorings like plates left
overnight in a sink.
Mr. Aurelio Furtado was ninety pounds of man under a
blanket the color of weak tea. His daughter stood by the
radiator with her coat still zipped. She was perhaps
fifty, with his long jaw, and she held out three sheets
of lined paper folded into a square so small it looked
as if it had been carried in a shoe. "He wrote it last
month," she said. "Before. He wants it read to me while
he can still hear it." She paused. "I don't speak it. I
never did. He made sure of that."
Behind my badge, on the same lanyard, I keep a
laminated card with the code of ethics. Canon one:
render the message faithfully, without addition,
omission, or distortion. I have held to it in
depositions and emergency rooms, through a woman's
miscarriage and a roofer's drunk-driving plea. The
oxygen concentrator beside the bed took its long breaths
for him and let them out with a small complaint, as if
it, too, had been asked to work past its hours.
I unfolded the letter. His was the handwriting of
the island schools of seventy years ago, every capital a
little ship under sail. The first page was easy. "Dana,"
I read, "I am writing this because my mouth was never
good for it." He wrote about the house on Rua da Pena,
the fig tree that split the cistern, the boat he had
named for her grandmother and then sold. Dana kept her
arms folded. The English came out of me clean and plain,
and I could hear each sentence land on her and stay.
The second page was why he left. In Portuguese the
sentence was short. I went because I was happy with
Lurdes in a way I was never happy in your mother's
kitchen, and I would go again. I looked at it long
enough that Dana unfolded her arms. Faithfully, the card
said. Without omission. Without distortion. The
concentrator sighed. Out in the lot a plow went back and
forth across the same stretch of asphalt, scraping it
bare, scraping it bare.
"I went because I was afraid," I read. "Afraid of
the kitchen, afraid of being a father in a language I
did not have. I was a coward, and I would give anything
to go back." Dana's mouth did something it had not
decided to do. She sat on the edge of the bed carefully,
the way you sit on ice you don't trust.
The third page I read nearly as he wrote it: the
account at the Halsey Credit Union; his watch, which was
to go to a grandson he had met twice; a request that
they not bury him in a suit. Dana laughed at the suit,
once, wetly, and put her hand on the blanket where his
knee was. My voice was a borrowed coat, and I was
handing it back with something left in the pocket.
When I finished, Mr. Furtado's eyes were open. They
found me, not her. "Não foi isso que eu escrevi," he
said, in a voice like a page turning. That is not what I
wrote. "Eu sei," I said. I know. Dana looked up from his
knee. "What did he say?" The plow had stopped. Under my
badge the card lay flat against my chest. "He says I
read it well," I told her, and her father closed his
eyes, and whatever crossed his face on the way down, I
have not been able to name it.
