spec.premise: a clockmaker's daughter inherits a shop of stopped clocks

set.title: The Hours in Coldharbour Lane
set.headnote: The following passage is from a short story by Edith Marrable, set in an English market town shortly before the First World War.

characters: Nell Garrow, the narrator, a grown daughter
blueprint.setting: A clock shop in Coldharbour Lane, an English town, March 1912
blueprint.situation: Nell, who left home for Bristol, returns after her father's death intending to sell his shop of stopped clocks; she finds a ledger showing each clock was stopped at an hour from her life.
blueprint.conflict: Nell's professed practicality and sense of having been neglected versus the evidence of her father's silent, devoted attention.
blueprint.central_idea: Love that seems displaced onto objects may be a hidden form of attention; the narrator can admit its effect on her only in practical terms.
blueprint.complexity: Both father and daughter misread each other: he believed she did not look back, she believed he did not look at her. The narrator's insistence on practicality is undercut by her actions, and the stopped clocks shift from commercial defect to memorial.
blueprint.speaker: Nell, first person, retrospective, guarded and self-deceiving about her feeling

devices.quote: I was never sentimental about clocks
devices.function: Professed detachment that the ending undercuts.

devices.quote: every one had stopped
devices.function: Stopped clocks first signal loss and lower value, later preserved hours of her life.

devices.quote: like a row of deacons who had forgotten the hymn
devices.function: Gives the silent clocks a solemn, faintly comic awkwardness.

devices.quote: held its pendulum still, as a man holds his breath
devices.function: Makes the shop seem to keep a deathbed vigil.

devices.quote: Dust had settled on the glass in a fine grey fur
devices.function: Conveys neglect and suspended time.

devices.quote: When I was a girl I was permitted in the shop
devices.function: Establishes her sense of marginality before the ledger revises it.

devices.quote: "Hush, Nell," he would say, though I had said nothing
devices.function: Shows the father's half-absent attention.

devices.quote: It was always a clock that was nearly going
devices.function: Reinforces her grievance that clocks came first.

devices.quote: his own watch ticked so loudly in that silent room
devices.function: Sets commercial running time against the shop's held hours.

devices.quote: I find I'm not ready to sell
devices.function: Marks the reversal of her businesslike resolve.

shifts.quote: found instead a little cash book
shifts.from: brisk commercial detachment
shifts.to: discovery and unsettlement

shifts.quote: I find I'm not ready to sell
shifts.from: intention to sell
shifts.to: keeping the clocks as they are

blueprint.form_notes: Seven paragraphs, retrospective first person; the final sentence recasts the practical stance.

provenance.note: Original passage written for practice use.

stanzas: My father died on a Tuesday in March of 1912, and by
Thursday I had decided to sell the shop. I set this down
first so it will be understood that I was never
sentimental about clocks. There were forty-one of them
on the walls of the shop in Coldharbour Lane, and every
one had stopped.
He had stopped them himself, I supposed, in the last
week, when his hands grew too uncertain for the winding.
That was like him: he would rather have a clock silent
than wrong. The bracket clocks stood along the counter
like a row of deacons who had forgotten the hymn, and
the long-case by the door held its pendulum still, as a
man holds his breath outside a sickroom. Dust had
settled on the glass in a fine grey fur. I did not wipe
it. A dealer does not pay more for clean glass.
When I was a girl I was permitted in the shop only
on Saturdays, and only to sit on the stool by the stove
and not touch. My father bent over his bench with the
loupe screwed into his eye, so that he looked at me,
when he looked at all, with one eye enormous and one eye
small. "Hush, Nell," he would say, though I had said
nothing. "She's nearly going." He meant a clock. It was
always a clock that was nearly going.
Mr. Pell came at eleven, a brisk man in a brown
overcoat with a chain across his waistcoat, and his own
watch ticked so loudly in that silent room that I could
hear it from the counter. He walked the walls, lifting
dials, naming prices under his breath. "Forty for the
lot," he said. "They're none of them running, Miss
Garrow. You understand that brings it down." "I
understand perfectly," I said.
It was while he was in the back room, measuring the
long-case, that I opened the drawer of the bench to find
the winding keys, and found instead a little cash book
with its columns ruled for shillings and pence. My
father had not used it for money. Each line held the
name of a clock, and beside it an hour, and beside that
a few words in his small upright hand. The Dutch
bracket, ten past four: N. born. The French carriage
clock, a quarter to nine: N. walks to the stove alone.
The long-case, twenty past six: N. says Father, not Da.
There were forty-one lines. The last was the little
enamel clock in the window, eleven minutes past two: N.
leaves for Bristol on the coach, does not look back.
I looked up. The enamel clock said eleven minutes
past two. I had looked back; I am quite certain of it. I
had looked back at the window, and the window had been
full of clocks, and I had not seen him behind them.
Mr. Pell returned with his tape. "Forty-five, then,
as the long-case is sound." "I find I'm not ready to
sell," I said. "Not at present. You'll forgive me the
trouble." He looked at me as if I were a mechanism with
a part missing, and then he went out, and his watch went
with him, and the shop was quiet again. I put the cash
book in my coat. I have not wound any of them. It is a
practical matter: one would have to know which hour to
set them to, and I find that I know all of them.

items.stem: Which of the following statements is the most defensible thesis about the passage as a whole?

options.text: Through a narrator who insists on her practicality, the passage shows that a father's absorption in clocks hid a close attention to his daughter that she can admit only indirectly.
options.label: correct
options.why: Accounts for the ledger, the narrator's guarded voice, and the practical ending.

options.text: Through the clock shop's decline, the passage argues that small family trades of the period were doomed by the dealers who bought up their stock at low prices.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Pell is incidental; no argument about trade is made.

options.text: Through the father's ledger, the passage shows that the narrator was right to believe her father cared more for his clocks than for her own company.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The ledger shows the opposite: his clocks recorded her.

options.text: Through its many images of time, the passage suggests that every human memory is uncertain and that no past event can ever be known with confidence.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Overgeneralizes one disputed memory into a universal claim.

evidence_quotes: N. leaves for Bristol on the coach, does not look back.
I had not seen him behind them.

spec.premise: a young apprentice delivers a repaired watch to the house of a customer who never pays

set.title: The Danner Account
set.headnote: The following passage is from a short story by Lowell Imbrie, set in a small mill town shortly after the Second World War.

characters: the narrator, looking back on himself at fifteen as a watchmaker's apprentice
Mrs. Ilse Danner, a widowed customer whose son was lost in the war
blueprint.setting: Canal Street and Tanner Hill in a small mill town, winter of 1951
blueprint.situation: The apprentice carries a watch that comes in for 'repair' every month to a customer who never pays, intending to demand money; he finds a house of stopped clocks and a mother who lets her dead son's watch run down so she can bring it back.
blueprint.conflict: The boy's belief that the world runs on payment against the unspoken arrangement of grief and mercy between Mrs. Danner and Mr. Pruitt; also the boy's inner conflict between his rehearsed demand and his silence.
blueprint.central_idea: What looks like an unpaid debt is a silent act of mercy; some accounts are kept in a currency the young narrator cannot yet read.
blueprint.complexity: The narrator both learns and refuses to learn: he discovers Pruitt has been paying, yet as an adult still claims he would have asked for the money. Mrs. Danner's ritual is both denial and a way of continuing; Pruitt's ledger turns charity into bookkeeping so it can be given without being named.

devices.quote: like a doctor listening to a chest he already knew was sound
devices.function: Shows Pruitt knows the watch is not broken and is attending to something other than mechanism.

devices.quote: It sat in my mouth like a coin
devices.function: Makes the demand for payment a physical burden the boy cannot spend.

devices.quote: leaned toward the street as if it were trying to hear
devices.function: Makes the house seem to strain toward news, like a waiting mother.

devices.quote: whose pendulum hung dead as a plumb line
devices.function: Part of the cluster of stopped clocks expressing time halted by grief.

devices.quote: the story of Penelope, who wove a shroud by day
devices.function: Frames Mrs. Danner's undoing of the watch as a ritual of waiting for someone who will not return.

devices.quote: a man's steel Hesper with a cracked strap
devices.function: The watch stands for the lost son and for the time she will not let run on.

devices.quote: the river ran blue on one side and rust on the other
devices.function: Divided landscape mirrors the boy's split between demand and pity.

devices.quote: I still tell people I would have asked her
devices.function: The adult narrator clings to the hard pose the story has undone.

devices.quote: and then I bring it to him because it is broken
devices.function: Mrs. Danner plainly states her ritual, revealing she knows the watch is not broken.

blueprint.speaker: First-person retrospective narrator, now an adult shopkeeper
blueprint.form_notes: Seven paragraphs; delayed reveal in the final paragraph; closing sentence returns to the adult present.

stanzas: In the winter of 1951 I was fifteen and believed
that the world ran on payment, the way Mr. Abelard
Pruitt's shop ran on the long brass pendulum that hung
in the window and told the whole of Canal Street when it
was late. I swept, I sorted mainsprings by size into the
paper twists he folded for them, and on Thursdays I
carried finished work to the customers who could not or
would not come in. Mrs. Ilse Danner of Tanner Hill was
one who would not. Her page in the ledger was a long
column of entries, and I had looked down the column
marked received and found not one figure in it.
Every month the same watch came in, a man's steel
Hesper with a cracked strap, and every month Mr. Pruitt
took it to the bench under the green lamp, opened the
back, and looked into it for a long time, like a doctor
listening to a chest he already knew was sound. Then he
cleaned it, closed it, and wrapped it in tissue.
"Danner," he would say, handing it to me. "Put it on the
account." I had decided the account was a joke he played
on himself.
That Thursday I had made up my mind to ask her for
the money. I rehearsed it on the walk up the hill, past
the dye works, where the river ran blue on one side and
rust on the other, and the sentence got smoother each
time I turned it over: Mr. Pruitt asks if you could
settle something on the account, ma'am. I did not intend
to say ma'am in any soft way.
Her house leaned toward the street as if it were
trying to hear what was said about it. Inside it was
colder than the porch. There was a mantel clock with its
hands at twenty past four, a cuckoo clock with its
little door shut, a tall case clock in the hall whose
pendulum hung dead as a plumb line. I counted five
clocks, and not one of them was going. She took the
tissue from me and unwrapped the watch the way you would
unwind a bandage.
"Does it run?" she asked. "Yes, ma'am. Mr. Pruitt
says it keeps good time." "It always does, when it comes
back." She held it to her ear, then laid it face down on
the oilcloth. "I wind it, and in a few days I forget to
wind it, and it stops, and then I bring it to him
because it is broken." She said this plainly, as a woman
might explain why she salts the walk. I had my sentence
ready. It sat in my mouth like a coin.
On the sideboard was a photograph of a boy in a
sailor's collar, not much older than I was, and beside
it a folded flag with the stiffness of a thing nobody
touches. I thought of the story of Penelope, who wove a
shroud by day and unpicked it by night so the suitors
would have to go on waiting and her husband might still
come home. Mrs. Danner was not weaving anything. She was
only letting a watch run down. "You wanted to say
something," she said. "No, ma'am," I said. "He says it's
good for another month."
I walked down the hill in the dark with the money
unasked for and told myself it was because she had
cried, though she had not cried. At the shop Mr. Pruitt
was closing the ledger, and I looked over his arm at her
page. I had searched that column for figures. Beside
every entry, in his small upright hand, was a word I had
not been looking for: Paid. And after it, every time,
his own initials. I keep a shop of my own now, and I
still tell people I would have asked her.

items.stem: Which of the following thesis statements offers the most defensible interpretation of the passage as a whole?

options.text: The passage suggests that a debt rooted in grief may be settled in silence, so that what looks like a swindle proves to be quiet mercy.

options.text: The passage argues that commerce in small towns always gives way to kindness, since every merchant secretly forgives the debts of his neighbors.
options.label: too_broad

options.text: The passage shows a grieving widow who manipulates a soft-hearted watchmaker, exploiting his pity to avoid paying for repeated repairs.
options.label: unsupported

options.text: The passage recounts how an apprentice carries a watch up a hill, meets a customer, and returns to find entries written in a ledger.

spec.premise: an innkeeper and a stranger bargain over a room on the night before a wedding

set.title: The Kitchen Room
set.headnote: The following scene is from The Kitchen Room, a play by Ruth Abernathy Kell, set in a small lake-town hotel in the early 1950s.

characters: VERA HOLLIS, fifties, keeper of the Gannet House, whose daughter marries tomorrow
THE STRANGER (WALT PELL), her husband, who left the family eighteen years earlier
blueprint.setting: The front desk of the Gannet House, a narrow hotel in the lake town of Port Ellery, near midnight in late May, early 1950s; paper wedding bells hang from the light fixture.
blueprint.situation: A traveler with a cardboard suitcase asks for a room in a hotel full of wedding guests. He raises his offer bill by bill while the keeper refuses, until she names a price of twelve dollars and calls him by name. She has known him from the moment he shut the door.
blueprint.conflict: Walt wants some place, however small, at his daughter's wedding; Vera wants to protect the day and refuses him the standing of family, yet she cannot quite turn him away.
blueprint.central_idea: Money stands in for an obligation that can never be paid; Vera can let Walt in only as a paying stranger, so that her concession and her refusal turn out to be the same act.
blueprint.complexity: Vera's refusal is real and so is her tenderness: she remembers his habit with the door and echoes it at the end, she gives him her daughter's old room, and she keeps his money for the wedding rather than the till. Walt asks for little, 'only' to see the bride, but his last question shows that he hopes for more. Even the reckoning is done in the language of a hotel bill.

devices.quote: stacked in the parlor like cordwood
devices.function: Walt's wry comparison casts the wedding guests as goods in storage and establishes his outsider's humor.

devices.quote: It's hot as a mouth till four in the morning
devices.function: Makes the offered room sound uninviting and close, a grudging concession dressed as a warning.

devices.quote: The house is asleep.
devices.function: Vera's closing line repeats Walt's old habit of treating the house as a sleeper, so intimacy surfaces even as she dismisses him.

devices.quote: It's eighteen years at nothing a year, Walt.
devices.function: Turns the price of the room into a bill for his years of absence and recasts the haggling as a reckoning.

devices.quote: she lays it face down without looking up
devices.function: The photograph stands for the family life Vera guards; turning it face down and face up again shows her ambivalence.

devices.quote: Another bill.
devices.function: The bills set down one after another make the scene's measure of value, and of what cannot be paid, visible on stage.

devices.quote: Breakfast is at six for family. You're not family.
devices.function: Sets the household against the outsider and spells out the terms on which she admits him.

devices.quote: He eases the door shut so it will not bang.
devices.function: Plants the habit by which Vera recognized him, which pays off when she reveals that she knew him.

devices.quote: Five dollars is a fair price for a full house.
devices.function: Walt haggles as if over a room when the real cost is far greater, irony the audience feels once his identity comes out.

devices.quote: I know what it was.
devices.function: Her clipped past tense treats his name, and his marriage, as finished.

devices.quote: It's eighteen years at nothing a year, Walt.
devices.function: The flat bargaining tone gives way to open, personal reckoning.

shifts.quote: It's eighteen years at nothing a year, Walt.
shifts.from: impersonal haggling between keeper and traveler
shifts.to: open reckoning between estranged husband and wife

shifts.quote: Mind the door going up. The house is asleep.
shifts.from: terse dismissal
shifts.to: a guarded echo of shared intimacy

blueprint.form_notes: Single-scene drama with stage directions. The speech headings change from STRANGER to WALT once Vera names him. The scene closes on a wordless stage direction.
blueprint.speaker: Dramatic; no narrator. Stage directions supply gestures the characters do not explain.

provenance.note: Original scene written for practice; author and play are invented.

stanzas: (The front desk of the Gannet House, a narrow hotel
in Port Ellery. Near midnight, late May. A radiator
knocks, though the season is long past needing it. Paper
bells hang crooked from the light fixture. Behind the
desk VERA HOLLIS, fifties, writes in a ledger. A framed
photograph stands at her elbow; when the street door
opens, she lays it face down without looking up. The
STRANGER enters: a man about her age, a cardboard
suitcase, a good hat gone soft at the brim. He eases the
door shut so it will not bang.)
STRANGER. Evening. I'd like a room.
VERA. We're full. There's a wedding.
STRANGER. So I saw. Bells on the door, bells on the
lamp. Somebody in this town owns a lot of crepe paper.
(He sets the suitcase down as if it lives there.) One
night. I don't need a view.
VERA. Nobody gets a view. The lake's on the other
side of the cannery. (She turns a page.) The Lindqvist
place on Water Street might have a cot.
STRANGER. I tried the Lindqvist place. They've got
the groom's people stacked in the parlor like cordwood.
(He takes out a wallet and lays a bill on the open
ledger.) I'm in pumps. Sump pumps, well pumps. I go
where the water is.
VERA. (She slides the bill off the ledger with the
end of her pen, as if it might stain the page.) Then go
to the lake.
STRANGER. Five dollars is a fair price for a full
house. (Another bill.) Seven is generous.
VERA. Seven is what my rooms cost in August, with
breakfast. It's May. I'm full.
STRANGER. Everybody has a room they don't count. A
sewing room. A room where the roof leaks and the bed's
got one short leg. (A third bill.) Ten. I'll sleep on
the short side.
VERA. (She opens the drawer of keys. She does not
take one out. She closes it.) There's a room over the
kitchen. The stovepipe runs through it. It's hot as a
mouth till four in the morning. (He waits.) It was my
daughter's room. She's in the good front room tonight,
with her dress hung on the closet door so it won't
crease. Tomorrow she's somebody's wife, and the kitchen
room goes back to being nobody's. (Pause.) Twelve
dollars.
STRANGER. (Slowly he counts out two more bills. His
hand stays on them.) Twelve. That's a funny number.
VERA. It's eighteen years at nothing a year, Walt. I
rounded down.
WALT. (He takes off his hat at last. The radiator
knocks twice and goes quiet.) When did you know?
VERA. When you shut the door so it wouldn't bang.
You always did that. Like the house was asleep and you
were the only one decent enough to let it be. (She turns
the photograph up, looks at it, lays it face down
again.) Pumps.
WALT. I was in pumps. For a while. (Beat.) I only
want to see her walk in. I'd sit in the last pew and
nobody would turn around.
VERA. Everybody turns around at a wedding. That's
what the aisle is for.
WALT. Then I'll stand outside and watch the doors.
VERA. (She dips her pen and writes in the ledger,
carefully, as for any guest.) Name.
WALT. You know my name.
VERA. I know what it was. (She writes.) W. Pell.
Pumps. One night. (She takes a key from the drawer and
lays it on the money, not in his hand.) The back stairs.
Breakfast is at six for family. You're not family. The
bus to Carrow leaves at seven-ten.
WALT. (He picks up the key and leaves the money
where it lies.) And if I miss the bus?
VERA. Then you'll be one more man in this town who
missed something. (She closes the ledger.) Mind the door
going up. The house is asleep. (He goes. She sits a long
while. She turns the photograph over and looks at it;
then she squares the bills into a stack and puts them,
not in the till, but in the pocket of her apron, the one
that holds the pins for tomorrow's hem.)

items.stem: Vera's short sentences in her reply ([[r1]]) primarily convey her

options.text: determination to treat the encounter as plain business, answering each raised offer with flat fact rather than feeling
options.label: correct
options.why: Three clipped statements of price, month and occupancy turn his offer into a matter of fact. She gives no emotion away, and she keeps this guard up until she names him.

options.text: open contempt for the stranger's trade, which she mocks by comparing his offer to the cheap rates of the off-season
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Her tone is flat, not openly contemptuous. She is not mocking pumps here, and August is her high season, not a cheap one.

options.text: growing willingness to bargain, since her mention of August prices invites him to name a figure closer to that rate
options.label: reversal
options.why: She ends with 'I'm full,' which shuts the bargaining down rather than inviting a counteroffer.

options.text: pride in the Gannet House's summer trade, which she defends against a traveler who assumes her rooms are cheap
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: This option latches onto 'August' and 'rooms' as though the line were about the hotel's reputation. The sentences are about refusing him, not about pride in the business.

refs.quote: Seven is what my rooms cost in August, with breakfast

evidence_quotes: Seven is what my rooms cost in August, with breakfast. It's May. I'm full.

items.stem: The audience's sense that Walt's description of his work ([[r1]]) is not fully reliable is confirmed chiefly by

options.text: his later admission ([[r2]]), which recasts the trade as something past and only temporary
options.label: correct
options.why: Once he has been unmasked, Walt changes the present tense to 'was' and adds 'For a while,' which shows that his opening self-description was a cover.

options.text: Vera's dry repetition of the single word "Pumps," which proves that he has never sold a pump at all
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Her one-word echo does signal skepticism, but it does not prove he never sold pumps. He says he was in the trade 'For a while.'

options.text: the cardboard suitcase described at his entrance, which shows that he carries no samples of the goods he sells
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the play says what is in the suitcase. The detail suggests modest means, not a lie about his trade.

options.text: his offer of ever larger sums, which reveals that a pump salesman could never honestly carry so much cash
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The rising offers drive the bargaining and the motif of payment. The scene never questions where his money came from.

options.text: suggest Vera is distracted by wedding preparations and has forgotten the man before her

options.text: signal to the stranger that she will give in once he reaches the exact price she wants

items.stem: A student claims that Vera grants Walt shelter while refusing him the standing of a husband or father. Which commentary best explains how the stage direction ([[r1]]) supports this claim?

options.text: Setting the key on the bills rather than in his hand keeps even her concession a sale, sparing her the touch a reconciliation would require.
options.label: correct
options.why: The direction contrasts 'on the money' with 'not in his hand.' The room is granted as a transaction, and the personal contact that would admit him as family is withheld.

options.text: By setting the key on the bills, Vera shows that she cares more for the money than for Walt, confirming her only motive all night has been profit.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The gesture is transactional, but the ending shows money is not her motive: the bills go 'not in the till' but into the apron for the wedding.

options.text: By refusing to place the key in his hand, Vera makes clear that she still fears Walt, who once harmed her and might harm her daughter again.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the scene suggests he was violent or that she fears him. Her distance is about where he stands with the family, not about danger.

options.text: By laying the key down at last, Vera shows that she has forgiven Walt completely and now welcomes him back into the household as before.
options.label: reversal
options.why: She tells him 'You're not family' and gives him the time of the morning bus, which rules out a full welcome.

items.stem: The change in the speech headings from "STRANGER" to "WALT" after Vera's line ([[r1]]) primarily has which effect?

options.text: It shows that Walt has decided to reveal himself to Vera, ending a disguise he had planned to drop all along.
options.label: misread_speaker

options.text: It indicates that the audience knew the stranger's identity from the start and Vera alone is learning it now.

options.text: It suggests that Walt, once he is named, becomes a sympathetic figure whose motives can now be fully trusted.

items.stem: Which of the following statements is the most defensible thesis about the scene as a whole?

options.text: By staging a father's return as haggling over a room, the playwright suggests Vera can admit Walt only on terms that also shut him out.
options.label: correct
options.why: This is specific and arguable, and the scene supports it: she gives him a key and her daughter's old room but tells him 'You're not family.' The bargain is both admission and exclusion.

options.text: In the scene, a hotel keeper and a traveling salesman argue over the price of a room before she finally agrees to rent him her daughter's old room.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: This only summarizes the plot. It makes no claim and misses that the 'salesman' is her husband.

options.text: The playwright shows that money can never repair the damage of the past, a truth that every family must eventually face and accept.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: It turns the scene into a universal moral and loses the particular way Vera uses money to set terms.

options.text: Through the bargaining, the playwright shows Walt cunningly exploiting Vera's need for money until she must accept him back as her husband.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Vera controls the bargaining and the reveal, and she refuses him family standing rather than accepting him back.

items.stem: Vera's answer ([[r1]]) to Walt's question reveals which aspect of their relationship?

options.text: Beneath her resentment she still knows his small habits, recalling one with reluctant exactness.
options.label: correct
options.why: She recognized him by a gesture alone ('You always did that') and even calls it 'decent,' so intimacy survives inside the reckoning.

options.text: She has spent eighteen years waiting for his return and has privately rehearsed this exact meeting.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The scene shows recognition, not years of waiting or rehearsal. Nothing points to that.

options.text: She resents him chiefly for his carelessness, a fault she sees even in the way he enters a room.

options.why: The habit she remembers is a considerate one, shutting the door quietly, not a careless one.

options.text: She admires his courtesy so much that she is ready to forget the years he spent away from her family.

spec.premise: a village schoolteacher receives a visitor from the city ministry

set.title: from The Fen Parish
set.headnote: The following passage is from a nineteenth-century novel. The narrator has kept the village school of Hollin Cross since the death of her brother, its schoolmaster.

characters: Theodora Penhallow, narrator, sister of the late schoolmaster, who has secretly kept the school for six years
Mr. Dask, inspector from the Ministry of Instruction
Tobias Reck, Ann Marle, Hetty Gall, pupils
blueprint.setting: The parish schoolroom of Hollin Cross, a fen village, on a wet March Tuesday in the mid-nineteenth century
blueprint.situation: A ministry inspector arrives at a school the narrator has run under her dead brother's name; she claims the master is ill upstairs; a small child exposes her, and the inspector, rather than reporting her, approves the school 'under its present master' and leaves.
blueprint.conflict: The narrator's competence and devotion against Regulations that forbid a woman to keep a school; her fear of exposure against her pride in her work.
blueprint.central_idea: A deception maintained out of necessity can become a cage of its own; the narrator learns that what she guarded was less a secret than a dead man's place, and the inspector's quiet complicity frees her to occupy it.
blueprint.complexity: The inspector's ambiguous mercy: he enforces nothing and sanctions everything through irony, so official approval and rule-breaking coincide; the narrator's pride is tinged with guilt; the children are complicit witnesses; the coat shifts from relic to garment.

devices.quote: I brushed it as other women brush the stones
devices.function: Equates her care of the coat with mourning ritual, showing the fiction as a kind of grave-tending.

devices.quote: My brother's greatcoat hung on its peg
devices.function: The coat stands for the fiction of the absent master and, at the end, the role she takes on openly.

devices.quote: the stove sulked in its corner
devices.function: Gives the room a grudging, uneasy mood during the examination.

devices.quote: as a boat tilts when someone careless stands up in it
devices.function: Conveys the sudden instability of exposure.

devices.quote: shall Miss hear our spelling after, same as always?
devices.function: A child's innocent speech reveals the secret.

devices.quote: What had I to fear? Only the end of everything.
devices.function: Renders her panic and stakes from inside her thought.

devices.quote: I trust Mr. Penhallow's chest will hold until then.
devices.function: Dask's mock-concern signals he knows and will collude.

devices.quote: I had only been keeping a coat
devices.function: Redefines the secret as mere preservation of an empty form.

devices.quote: Nobody laughed. Nobody breathed.
devices.function: Moves from growing pride to suspended dread.

devices.quote: which I had never sat in
devices.function: Contrasts with her sitting in his chair at the end.

shifts.to: guilty pride

blueprint.speaker: Theodora Penhallow, narrating retrospectively in the first person
blueprint.form_notes: Eight paragraphs, retrospective first person, period diction, quiet ironic turn at the close.

stanzas: The inspector came on a Tuesday in March, when the
dyke-water stood level with the road and the whole
parish of Hollin Cross smelt of wet rope and turned
earth. I had been expecting him for six years, which is
to say that I had ceased to expect him at all. My
brother's greatcoat hung on its peg beside the
schoolroom door, where it had hung since the winter he
died, and every Saturday I brushed it as other women
brush the stones of a grave.
He was a narrow gentleman in a grey muffler, and he
carried a portmanteau that looked better fed than he
did. He asked, with his hat already in his hand, whether
he might see Mr. Penhallow. I told him what I had told
the curate, the carrier, and six years of letters from
the Ministry of Instruction, all answered in a hand that
had once been my brother's and was now mine: that the
master was confined above stairs with his chest, and
could not come down, but that the school was entirely at
the gentleman's disposal.
'Then I shall not trouble him,' said Mr. Dask.
'Children are the better witnesses, as a rule. They have
not yet learned what is wanted.'
He sat in my brother's chair, which I had never sat
in, and the stove sulked in its corner as it always did
when the wind came off the fen. Tobias Reck gave him the
rivers of the kingdom in order, down to the smallest.
Ann Marle worked a sum in compound interest upon the
slate and did not once look at me. Mr. Dask said 'Good'
to each of them in the same low voice, as though he were
counting coins and found none of them false. I began,
God forgive me, to be proud.
It was little Hetty Gall, who was five and sat
nearest the stove for warmth, who put up her hand.
'Please, sir,' she said, 'shall Miss hear our spelling
after, same as always?' Nobody laughed. Nobody breathed.
I felt the floor of that room tilt beneath me, as a boat
tilts when someone careless stands up in it, and I saw
Mr. Dask write a single line in his book.
What had I to fear? Only the end of everything. The
Regulations were plain as the Commandments: a parish
school was to be kept by a certificated master, and a
woman might assist but not keep it. Twelve pounds a
year, the cottage, the coals, the coat upon its peg; all
of it was held for a man who had lain six winters in the
churchyard. I had been so careful. I had been careful
even of the coat.
He buttoned his muffler at the door and looked a
while at the greatcoat. 'A good coat,' he said. 'It
wants wearing, Miss Penhallow, or the moth will have
it.' Then, drawing on his gloves: 'I have entered the
school as satisfactory under its present master. I am
expected again in three years, if the Ministry keeps me
so long. I trust Mr. Penhallow's chest will hold until
then.' He bowed, quite gravely, and went out to the
carrier's cart.
I stood a long while with my hand upon the latch.
For six years I had believed that I was keeping a
secret; I understood now that I had only been keeping a
coat. When the children had gone out to their dinners I
lifted it down from the peg. It was heavier than I
remembered, and smelt of camphor and of him, and I put
it on, and when they came back I sat in his chair, and
heard the spelling.

spec.premise: two brothers sit through a funeral meal without speaking

set.title: from The Short Field
set.headnote: The following passage is from Lise Marchuk's novel The Short Field (2019). The narrator has driven home to the prairies for his father's funeral.

characters: Teddy, the narrator, younger brother who left for Calgary
Nick, older brother who stayed on the family farm
blueprint.setting: Parish hall of St. Volodymyr's in a small Saskatchewan town, a February afternoon, after a father's funeral
blueprint.situation: Two estranged brothers sit side by side at their father's funeral lunch and do not speak.
blueprint.conflict: Teddy's pride and guilt against his wish to reconnect; he insists Nick never makes the first move while Nick's gestures suggest otherwise.
blueprint.central_idea: Estrangement can be sustained by the person who believes he is only waiting; love may be offered in small wordless acts that a defensive eye refuses to read.
blueprint.complexity: Teddy's narration is fair-sounding but self-justifying; the reader sees Nick's overtures (the moved parka, the salt shaker, the name card, eleven years of birthday cards) before Teddy admits them, and Teddy's hidden guilt (hanging up on the ward) surfaces quietly. The ending reverses his claim about who reaches out.

devices.quote: ticked like it was thinking about something
devices.function: Personifies the urn, making the silence feel watched and tense.

devices.quote: He has never once in his life made the first move.
devices.function: Claim contradicted by Nick's gestures and the name card.

devices.quote: the salt shaker stood like a small white chess piece
devices.function: Salt links Nick to their father and becomes an unclaimed offer between the brothers.

devices.quote: When I was twelve he salted a slice of birthday cake
devices.function: Reveals Teddy's old sense of exclusion from the father-Nick bond.

devices.quote: I thought about saying, Who's got the dog.
devices.function: Shows the many words Teddy rehearses but withholds.

devices.quote: not understanding the joke and understanding it perfectly
devices.function: Captures the child's exclusion: he grasps that the joke belongs to others.

devices.quote: the snow under them went the yellow of old teeth
devices.function: Bleak, aging imagery for mourning and time lost.

devices.quote: Instead I ate a pickle. It was very good.
devices.function: Flat retreat into trivia in place of speech.

shifts.quote: Someone had written my name on it, TEDDY
shifts.from: defensive stalemate and self-justification
shifts.to: recognition that Nick has been reaching out all along

blueprint.speaker: Teddy, first person, retrospective but close to the moment
blueprint.form_notes: Seven paragraphs; plain contemporary first-person voice; ending recasts the narrator's claims.

stanzas: The church ladies of St. Volodymyr's had put us at
the end of the long table, under the felt banner of the
Holy Family, beside the coffee urn that ticked like it
was thinking about something. Nick was already there
when I came in from the parking lot. He had his parka on
the chair next to him, and when he saw me he moved it to
the floor, which I took to mean he had wanted the chair
for his feet and changed his mind.
I want to be fair. I had driven nine hours from
Calgary in February, through Medicine Hat and Swift
Current and every flat white mile of it, and I had not
come to fight. Nick had stayed. Nick had the farm, the
dog, the hospital visits, forty years of Dad's opinions
about the weather. I had a condo and a job selling
irrigation software to people who used to be his
neighbours. That was the arrangement, and it was
nobody's fault, and anyway I wasn't going to be the one
to speak first. He has never once in his life made the
first move.
The food came on in waves. Holubtsi in a roaster
pan. Perogies glistening with onion. A ham, a pink
jellied salad with grapes suspended in it like flies in
amber, and a plate of dill pickles that someone had cut
lengthwise with a precision I found almost hostile. Mrs.
Hrynchuk leaned between us and said, "Your father loved
my beet salad," and Nick said, "He did," and I said, "He
did," and she went away satisfied, as though she had
married us.
Nick salted his perogies before he tasted them. Dad
did that. Dad salted fried eggs, cantaloupe, beer. When
I was twelve he salted a slice of birthday cake to make
Nick laugh, and Nick laughed so hard milk came out his
nose, and I sat there not understanding the joke and
understanding it perfectly. Now Nick set the shaker
down, not in the middle of the table where it belonged,
but six inches from my plate. I left it there. I don't
salt.
Across the hall, our cousin Darlene was telling the
story about the combine and the gopher again. People
laughed in the right places. The urn ticked. Outside the
window the parking lot lights came on one by one, though
it was barely four, and the snow under them went the
yellow of old teeth.
I thought about saying, You look tired. I thought
about saying, Who's got the dog. I thought about saying,
I called the ward on the Tuesday, which was true, and I
hung up before the nurse came back, which was also true.
Instead I ate a pickle. It was very good. Nick buttered
a bun with the slow attention he used to give to
splicing baler twine, and he did not look up, and I did
not look up, and between us the salt shaker stood like a
small white chess piece no one was willing to move.
When the ladies began clearing, I reached for my
coat and knocked over the folded card at my place.
Someone had written my name on it, TEDDY, in blue
ballpoint, the T with a little hook at the bottom. I
knew that hook. It was on every birthday card that had
come to Calgary for eleven years, the ones I put in the
drawer with the takeout menus. I looked down the table.
There were no other cards. Nobody else had been told
where to sit.
